analysis.one_liner: Bans auto insurers from using credit scores, education, occupation, and home ownership to set rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred auto insurers from pricing policies using income proxies like credit scores, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Car insurance is required by law in nearly every state, but insurers commonly set premiums using factors that have nothing to do with driving — credit scores, education level, job, employment status, whether you own a home, or which insurer you had before. The bill's findings section argues these are income proxies that charge lower-income drivers more and steer them to pricier affiliate companies. This bill would make it illegal for insurers or their affiliates to use any of those factors to set rates or decide who gets coverage, would force insurers' pricing rules to be open to public inspection instead of treated as trade secrets, and would let the FTC, state attorneys general, and individual drivers enforce the ban with fines and lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers with low credit scores, less education, unstable employment, or no home — disproportionately lower-income and younger people — who today pay higher premiums for the same driving record than drivers with more wealth and steadier jobs. Because insurance is legally mandatory in 49 states, these drivers cannot simply decline to buy coverage [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits auto insurers and their affiliates from considering education, occupation, employment status, home ownership, credit score, consumer reports, previous insurer, or prior purchase of insurance when setting rates or deciding eligibility [S2] [S3].

Deems it a violation whenever use of these factors prevents a consumer from getting the lowest rate available, receiving discounts, or keeping coverage — closing the common practice of steering drivers with weaker profiles into higher-priced affiliate companies [S3].
Requires all underwriting rules and rate filings to be open to public inspection, ending their treatment as proprietary trade secrets [S3].

Creates enforcement through the FTC (civil penalties of at least $2,500 per violation), private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees, and state attorneys general acting on behalf of residents [S3].
The bill's findings state that insurance is mandatory in 49 states, so drivers cannot escape higher premiums by declining coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Auto insurance companies lose a major pricing tool; credit reporting bureaus and related data sellers lose a large market, since insurers are significant buyers of credit scores and consumer reports. Some drivers with strong credit scores and homeownership who currently receive the steepest discounts could see rates move toward a driving-risk-only baseline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Auto insurers and credit data sellers

drawbacks.text: Insurers argue credit-based scores predict claims costs; stripping them could raise prices for drivers who benefit most from current credit discounts, meaning some better-off policyholders could pay more so others pay less [S3].

The bill requires insurers' underwriting rules and rate filings to be publicly available, which insurers treat as competitively sensitive — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, though the bill deems disclosure necessary for the public to verify compliance [S3].
The bill creates a broad private right of action with punitive damages and attorney's fees, which could generate litigation costs that insurers may pass on through premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is deliberate: it shifts part of the cost of mandatory car insurance from drivers with less wealth and steadier work to those with more, ending pricing based on factors other than driving. The strongest objection is that credit-based pricing may predict claims for some drivers, so customers who currently get large discounts could pay somewhat more. For the low-income drivers the bill targets, who cannot legally go without insurance, the benefit of paying premiums set by driving record rather than income proxies is substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Mrs. Watson Coleman introduced the bill on April 12, 2018, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Financial Services and the Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred [S5].
Congress.gov shows the bill with zero cosponsors for its entire life [S4].
The bill never became law; it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto insurers keep their ability to use credit scores, education, occupation, and home ownership in pricing, and credit bureaus keep insurer demand for their data. Lower-income drivers continue paying premiums shaped by those income proxies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Auto insurers and credit data sellers

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban income proxies in auto insurance pricing and referred it to two committees.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Financial Services and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action of any kind before the Congress ended.

against.name: Auto insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Insurers rely on credit scores, education, occupation, and home ownership in underwriting, all of which the bill would have prohibited; no industry support for the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable partisan split — though the two committees that buried it were both chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill bans the industry's common practice of pricing and steering customers using credit scores, education, occupation, employment status, and home ownership, and exposes its underwriting rules to public inspection. Insurers profit because these income proxies let them charge lower-income drivers more for legally mandatory coverage.

industries.industry: Credit reporting bureaus and consumer data sellers
industries.note: Insurers are major buyers of credit scores and consumer reports; the bill outlaws using them for auto insurance eligibility and pricing, removing a large revenue channel for the credit data industry.

industries.industry: Drivers with strong credit and homeownership
industries.note: These drivers currently receive the steepest discounts from credit- and status-based pricing and could pay more if rates are set on driving factors alone, though they also gain transparency into how rates are set.
